analysis.one_liner: Lets states no longer ban agreements requiring workers to join or pay a union.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would let union security agreements operate in all states, has sat in the House Education and Workforce Committee since September 2025 with no hearing, markup, or floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill repeals Section 14(b) of the National Labor Relations Act, the federal provision that lets states pass "right-to-work" laws. Right-to-work laws bar contracts that require workers to join a union or pay union fees as a condition of employment. Under the bill, unions and employers in any state could again agree to such requirements, which is widely reported to raise union membership and union finances, since unions must represent all workers in a bargaining unit whether or not those workers pay.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who join or would benefit from stronger unions gain the most: research consistently finds union members earn more and have better benefits than comparable non-union workers, and repealing state right-to-work laws would strengthen unions' ability to collect fees from the workers they represent. Unions themselves gain members and revenue in the roughly half of states with such laws.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Union members and would-be union workers

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the federal provision (NLRA Section 14(b)) that allows states to prohibit union security agreements, undoing state right-to-work laws nationwide.

Under the bill, unions and employers could negotiate contracts requiring workers in a bargaining unit to join the union or pay fees, ending the 'free rider' situation where unions must represent workers who pay nothing.

analysis.who_pays: Workers in right-to-work states who prefer not to join a union or pay fees could face that requirement as a condition of keeping their job, depending on what their union and employer negotiate. Employers lose a tool that keeps union membership and dues voluntary, and organized business groups have historically opposed such a change.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers and non-union workers who pay fees

drawbacks.text: The bill would allow union-and-employer contracts that require individual workers to join a union or pay fees to keep their jobs, removing the state-law protection workers in right-to-work states currently have against such requirements.

Opponents of right-to-work repeal argue mandatory fee arrangements can compel workers to financially support organizations whose politics they may not back, and that voluntary membership keeps unions more accountable to their members.
The bill would override the policy choices of the roughly half of states that have enacted right-to-work laws, raising a state-versus-federal control objection even for people sympathetic to unions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers who want stronger unions, the gain is real: unions with fee authority collect more resources and typically negotiate higher wages, and that benefit reaches non-union workers in heavily unionized industries too. The cost falls on individual workers who would prefer not to join or pay, and on employers who lose a lever they have used to limit union strength. Weighing it honestly, the bill is a straightforward transfer of bargaining power to organized labor and away from employers, sold on the wage evidence for union members and criticized for compelling dues from unwilling workers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled since.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Sherman introduced the bill on September 4, 2025, joined by 17 Democratic cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and Workforce the same day.
No further action — hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — appears in the action history through the end of the provided record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and businesses that benefit from state right-to-work laws are better off so far, because a bill that would end those laws nationwide has gone nowhere in committee. Union supporters have gained nothing yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who benefit from right-to-work laws

for.name: Rep. Brad Sherman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the federal provision allowing state right-to-work laws.

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, controlled by the Republican majority
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 4, 2025 and has taken no action on the bill since — no hearing or markup scheduled.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling House committees and floor scheduling
against.what_they_did: No Republican member cosponsored the bill, and the majority's committee system has left it without a hearing or vote.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 17 cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republican has cosponsored, and the bill sits in a Republican-controlled committee.

industries.note: Repealing state right-to-work authority would let unions collect fees from all workers they represent, boosting membership and revenue, which unions use to organize and bargain. That strength is the mechanism behind the higher wages and benefits union members earn.

Employers would lose the ability to operate under state right-to-work laws and could face contracts requiring union membership or fees. Employer groups have historically defended these laws as keeping union dues voluntary and labor costs lower.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has 17 Democratic cosponsors and none from the Republican majority that controls the House and the Education and Workforce Committee. Bills referred to a hostile committee without bipartisan backing almost never get a hearing, let alone a floor vote; the realistic path is that it sits without action until this Congress ends in January 2027.
